transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I came in because... it's just getting really noticeable, you know? Like, people can actually see it happening. Sometimes I'm moving like I'm underwater. It takes me forever just to answer a question or even get out of a chair. It's like gravity is turned up or something. Which reminds me, my chair at work—I do customer service, mostly over the phone—and this chair they gave me is just terrible for my back. I told my supervisor, Greg, that the lumbar support is completely shot, but he just brushed it off. Greg's always like that, always worrying about the metrics and call times instead of, you know, actual human comfort. Anyway, if I'm not moving in slow motion, I'm doing the exact opposite. I'll be pacing around my apartment, just rubbing my hands together constantly, like I'm trying to shake off a really bad call with a screaming customer. You ever get those calls where the person is just yelling before you even say hello? It's wild. But yeah, the moving slow or the pacing... that's why I'm here.

How long have you been feeling this way? Have these symptoms been happening almost every day for at least two weeks, or are they more of a recent reaction to things like the chair or stressful calls at work?

Well, it's definitely not just a recent thing from the chair or the calls. I mean, I wish it was just the chair. But no, this whole moving slow and then pacing thing... it's been going on for a long time. Like, about two years and three months now. I know the exact timeline because it all started right after I got fired from my last customer support job. Which, by the way, was completely unfair. They said my "call resolution times" were slipping, but I was actually taking the time to talk to the older customers, you know? Like this one lady, Mrs. Higgins, she would call in just because she couldn't figure out her router, but she really just wanted to talk about her grandson who was studying marine biology in Florida. I mean, how are you supposed to just cut someone off when they're talking about manatees? Manatees are fascinating, they're like sea cows. But yeah, management didn't care about manatees. They just cared about the timer. So they let me go, and right after that... that's when all this started. It's been over two years of this.
Have you noticed that things you used to enjoy, like talking to customers or hobbies outside of work, don’t interest you as much anymore?

Yeah, actually. It's... it's like a switch flipped. I used to do a lot of sketching, you know? Like, little charcoal drawings of people I'd see at coffee shops. I kept this whole notebook where I'd write down tasting notes for different roasts, too. I was really getting into Ethiopian blends for a while, the ones with those bright, fruity notes. Some of them almost taste like blueberry if they're roasted right. There was this one cafe down the street from my old apartment—before the rent got hiked up and I had to move to this place with the terrible plumbing—they had this pour-over setup that looked like a science experiment. The barista, I think her name was Chloe, she had this tattoo of a French press on her forearm that was really well done. But anyway... yeah, I used to love doing that, or going on weekend hikes up at the state park. Now? I just... I open the notebook, or I lace up my hiking boots, and I just feel... nothing. There's no pull. I just sit there staring at the boots and wonder what the point even is. Speaking of boots, I really need to get new laces for them, the left one is completely frayed from when my neighbor's dog chewed on it in the hallway. He’s a golden retriever mix, super friendly, but he chews everything.
Have you felt down or lost interest in things most of the time over the past two years?

Yeah, pretty much. Most of the time since this all started, it's just... it's like this heavy blanket, you know? The sadness, feeling guilty about losing that job, not caring about my coffee or my sketches, tossing and turning all night... it's always there in the background. Even if some weeks are a little lighter than others, it's still hanging around. Kind of like the smell in my new apartment building. It's this weird mix of boiled cabbage and old carpet. I've tried everything—candles, those plug-in air fresheners, even leaving the window open, which is a terrible idea because the street noise is ridiculous. There's this garbage truck that comes at exactly 4:15 AM on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the brakes squeal so loud it sounds like a metal monster dying. I actually called the city about it once, and they transferred me to three different departments before someone just hung up on me. It's funny, being on the other side of a customer service call. But yeah, the feeling down and losing interest... it's been pretty constant for the whole two years.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms, including persistent sadness, loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, and psychomotor disturbances (both slowing and restlessness), have been present for over two years with no mention of a prior major depressive episode, supporting a diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia). This rules out F32.2 (recurrent major depressive disorder, current episode severe without psychotic features) as there is no evidence of discrete episodes of major depression.
